CHAPTER XXXV

Gerard awoke, and found Denys watching him with some anxiety.

“It is you for sleeping! Why, 'tis high noon.”

“It was a blessed sleep,” said Gerard; “methinks Heaven sent it me. It
hath put as it were a veil between me and that awful night. To think
that you and I sit here alive and well. How terrible a dream I seem to
have had!”

“Ay, lad, that is the wise way to look at these things when once they
are past, why, they are dreams, shadows. Break thy fast, and then thou
wilt think no more on't. Moreover, I promised to bring thee on to the
town by noon, and take thee to his worship.”

Gerard then sopped some rye bread in red wine and ate it to break his
fast: then went with Denys over the scene of combat, and came back
shuddering, and finally took the road with his friend, and kept peering
through the hedges, and expecting sudden attacks unreasonably, till they
reached the little town. Denys took him to “The White Hart”.

“No fear of cut-throats here,” said he. “I know the landlord this many
a year. He is a burgess, and looks to be bailiff. 'Tis here I was making
for yestreen. But we lost time, and night o'ertook us--and--

“And you saw a woman at the door, and would be wiser than a Jeanneton;
she told us they were nought.”

“Why, what saved our lives if not a woman? Ay, and risked her own to do
it.”

“That is true, Denys; and though women are nothing to me, I long to
thank this poor girl, and reward her, ay, though I share every doit in
my purse with her. Do not you?”

“Parbleu.”

“Where shall we find her?”

“Mayhap the alderman will tell us. We must go to him first.”

The alderman received them with a most singular and inexplicable
expression of countenance. However, after a moment's reflection, he wore
a grim smile, and finally proceeded to put interrogatories to Gerard,
and took down the answers. This done, he told them that they must
stay in the town till the thieves were tried, and be at hand to give
evidence, on peril of fine and imprisonment. They looked very blank at
this.

“However,” said he, “'twill not be long, the culprits having been taken
red-handed.” He added, “And you know, in any case you could not leave
the place this week.”

Denys stared at this remark, and Gerard smiled at what he thought the
simplicity of the old gentleman in dreaming that a provincial town of
Burgundy had attraction to detain him from Rome and Margaret.

He now went to that which was nearest both their hearts.

“Your worship,” said he, “we cannot find our benefactress in the town.”

“Nay, but who is your benefactress?”

“Who? why the good girl that came to you by night and saved our lives at
peril of her own. Oh sir, our hearts burn within us to thank and bless
her; where is she?”

[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. I existed within a microscopic empire of two, subjugated by a man I was conditioned to call "Master." He was a square-built, brutal artifact of a world I did not know, roughly sixty years of age, though time on the island seemed measured only by the decay of his humanity. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER THREE.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

"Yes, I did; take my hand and lead me to the cabin."

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

"Bring the kid full of water," said he--"quick!"

I brought it, and he bathed his head and face. After a time, he threw himself back upon the bed-place, and groaned heavily.

"What's the matter, master?" said I.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

generated_text:
Gerard awoke to the sharp, anxious scrutiny of Denys, whose eyes betrayed a lingering unease. "It is you for sleeping! Why, 'tis high noon," Denys exclaimed, his voice cutting through the haze of Gerard's stupor.

"It was a blessed sleep," Gerard replied, his voice thick with relief. "Methinks Heaven sent it to me. It hath placed a veil between me and that awful night. To think that you and I sit here alive and well... How terrible a dream I seem to have had!"

"Ay, lad," Denys responded, his tone softening as he accepted the reality of their survival. "That is the wise way to view such things once they are past; they become merely dreams, fleeting shadows. Break thy fast, and thou shalt think no more on't. Moreover, I promised to bring thee to the town by noon, to present thee to his worship."

Gerard dipped a piece of coarse rye bread into a cup of red wine, consuming it to break his fast. Then, accompanied by Denys, he walked over the scarred landscape of the recent combat. He returned shuddering, the phantom weight of violence still clinging to his limbs, until they finally turned toward the road leading to the little town. As they traveled, Gerard kept peering anxiously through the hedgerows, expecting sudden ambushes with an unreasonable intensity, until the town gates came into view.

Denys led him straight to "The White Hart." "No fear of cut-throats here," Denys assured him, gesturing to the inn's sturdy facade. "I know the landlord; he has been a burgess for many a year and looks the part of a bailiff. 'Twas here I intended to make my stand yesterday evening. But we lost time, and night overtook us—and—"

"And you saw a woman at the door," Gerard interrupted, his heart leaping. "And would be wiser than a Jeanneton; she told us they were nought."

"Why, what saved our lives if not a woman?" Gerard pressed, his gratitude swelling like a tide. "Ay, and she risked her own life to do it."

"That is true, Denys," Gerard continued, his voice trembling with emotion. "Though women are nothing to me in battle, I long to thank this poor girl and reward her, ay, even though I share every doit in my purse with her. Do not you?"

"Parbleu," Denys agreed without hesitation.

"Where shall we find her?"

"Mayhap the alderman will tell us. We must go to him first."

The alderman received them with a countenance of singular and inexplicable gravity. However, after a moment's reflection, a grim smile softened his features, and he proceeded to interrogate Gerard, taking down their answers with meticulous care. Once finished, he informed them that they must remain in the town until the thieves were tried, requiring them to be at hand to give evidence under penalty of fine and imprisonment. They looked very blank at this decree, bewildered by the sudden confinement.

"However," the alderman said, dismissing their confusion, "'twill not be long; the culprits having been taken red-handed." He added, with a touch of bureaucratic finality, "And you know, in any case, you could not leave the place this week."

Denys stared at this remark, seemingly unable to grasp the logic, while Gerard smiled inwardly at what he perceived as the old gentleman's simplicity—the naive belief that a provincial town of Burgundy held any attraction capable of detaining men driven by the urgent summons of Rome and Margaret.

Now, Gerard turned to that which was nearest both their hearts. "Your worship," he said, bowing low, "we cannot find our benefactress in the town."

"Nay, but who is your benefactress?" the alderman asked, intrigued.

"Who? Why the good girl that came to you by night and saved our lives at peril of her own," Gerard declared, his passion rising. "Oh sir, our hearts burn within us to thank and bless her; where is she?"
